articles.content: Explanation: What color is the Moon? It depends on the night — and the time. Outside of the Earth’s atmosphere, the dark Moon, which shines by reflected sunlight, appears a magnificently brown-tinged gray. The featured image highlights a collection of apparent colors of the full moon on Earth, documented by one astrophotographer over 10 years from different locations across Italy. A red– or yellow-colored moon usually indicates a moon seen near the horizon. There, some of the blue light has been scattered away by a long path through the Earth’s atmosphere, sometimes laden with fine dust. A blue-colored moon is more rare and can indicate an atmosphere carrying larger dust particles. What created the purple moon is unclear — it may be a combination of several effects. The last image captures the total lunar eclipse of 2018 July — where the moon, in Earth’s shadow, appeared a faint red — due to light refracted through air around the Earth. Have you ever seen an unusually colorful Moon?

articles.author: Nurbek Bekmurzaev
articles.title: In Kazakhstan, rural women are forming collectives to improve their livelihoods
articles.excerpt: Their most pressing challenge is solving the long-standing water shortage in the village
articles.content:
This story by Nurbek Bekmurzaev originally appeared on Global Voices. Text licensed under CC BY 3.0. Reformatted for reading; third-party media omitted.

Their most pressing challenge is solving the long-standing water shortage in the village

This interview is part of a series of spotlights on the work of some of the grantees of the Digital Spark granting scheme, as part of the Regional Support Mechanism EECA project, implemented by the Metamorphosis Foundation and TechSoup, in partnership with CIVICUS and under the Digital Democracy Initiative (DDI) that covers the Global South. It is being published on Global Voices as part of a content-sharing agreement.  

Women in the rural areas of Kazakhstan are among those most affected by climate change, energy deficit, and poor governance. They bear the heavy burden of water shortages, especially in the southern parts of the country, where this problem is the most acute due to dense population, economic reliance on agriculture, and water losses related to outdated irrigation infrastructure.

In the village of Qyzylsay, located in the southern Jambyl region, the water shortage has become a major issue affecting the daily lives of women. It forces them to spend multiple hours a day outside their homes to secure water for their households, gardens, and animals. Their grueling work often goes unnoticed and unpaid, and their geographical remoteness places limits on access to information and government services, exacerbating their situation.

In 2026, Nazgul Aidabossynova, a local activist, implemented a project to help local women improve their livelihoods by training them to engage with the government more effectively and efficiently, calculate the cost of their labor and products, and mobilize collective efforts to solve community problems. Global Voices conducted an email interview with Aidabossynova to learn more about her initiative. The interview has been edited for clarity and brevity.

Global Voices (GV): Please tell us about your organization and why you chose to get involved with the Digital Sparks project.

Nazgul Aidabossynova (NA): I represent a community-based initiative led by rural women in Qyzylsay. Our work focuses on supporting women who manage households, small farms, livestock, and care responsibilities, while also facing limited access to information, public services, and opportunities for civic participation.

We chose to participate in the Digital Sparks project because digital tools can make a direct, practical difference in women’s daily lives. Many women already own smartphones, but previously used them mainly for calls and WhatsApp.

The project created an opportunity to turn these devices into tools for accessing eGov services, documenting community problems, managing farm and household responsibilities, protecting digital security, and communicating with local authorities.

GV: What issue/challenge in your community prompted you to undertake this project?

NA: The key challenge is unreliable access to water in Qyzylsay. Water often disappears from the pipes during the day, particularly in summer. This affects gardens, livestock, household work, and the health and well-being of families.

The burden falls disproportionately on women. They wake early to store water, carry water for household and agricultural needs, care for the livestock, and wait for irrigation turns. Much of this work is unpaid, time-consuming, and rarely recognized.

Women also faced barriers in reporting water problems: they knew what was happening, but often lacked the knowledge, evidence, and confidence needed to raise concerns effectively with local institutions.

GV: What are the key changes/activities that your organization implemented during your participation in the project?

NA: The project delivered four practical training sessions for ten rural women.

The first one, titled “Your Phone is More Than WhatsApp: Smartphone as Your Household Assistant”, taught them how to use smartphone reminders, photo-diaries for farm and livestock work, eGov services, strong passwords, and basic digital-security practices.

In the second workshop, titled “Smart Water: When Your Garden Tells You It’s Thirsty”, participants learned about water rights, the responsibilities of relevant local authorities, and water-supply mapping using timestamped and GPS-tagged photographs.

The third session, titled “Numbers Don’t Lie: When You Count Everything, You Earn More”, covered how to track unpaid work and calculate the real cost of agricultural products such as milk. It also discussed the economic value of time saved through smart irrigation.

In “Honest Agreement: When Technology Helps Us Trust Each Other”, the fourth and final session, participants prepared time-to-income plans, mapped local support networks, discussed peer mentoring, and agreed to begin work toward a cooperative approach to water advocacy and shared smart-irrigation infrastructure.

GV: How did your participation in the project impact your organization’s beneficiaries and the community that you serve? Please provide examples.

NA: The project helped participating women see smartphones as tools for independence, civic participation, and practical problem-solving, rather than only communication devices.

For example, women learned that they can use eGov services to request certain official documents online, reducing the need to spend time and money traveling to administrative offices.

They also learned to create structured evidence of water problems. A photograph of a dry canal, broken pipe, or contaminated water source becomes more useful for advocacy when it includes the date, location, and a written description.

The training on unpaid labor and production costs was especially meaningful. Participants calculated the value of their time and better understood the real cost of milk production and irrigation work. The discussion showed that manual irrigation may take up to 60 hours per month.

This helped participants recognize that their time has economic value, and that shared smart-irrigation solutions could create more time for income, education, rest, and community participation.

The group also began a peer-learning process. Three participants started sharing the knowledge gained during the training with neighboring women.

GV: How has your own knowledge, awareness, and experience with digital democracy and civic space changed, thanks to your participation in the project?

NA: My understanding of digital democracy has become much more practical. Before this project, digital tools could be viewed mainly as a way to communicate or access information.

Through Digital Sparks, I saw how digital tools can strengthen people’s ability to exercise rights, access public services, collect evidence, engage with local authorities, and organize collectively.

I also gained a stronger understanding of the link between digital inclusion, women’s unpaid labor, climate-related water challenges, and civic space.

For rural women, digital capacity is not only about technical skills. It is about having a voice, being able to document problems, understanding their rights, and participating in decisions that affect their families and community.

GV: What are the most valuable lessons and experiences you are taking away from this project?

NA: The most valuable lesson is that digital literacy has the greatest impact when it is directly connected to people’s real, daily needs. In Qyzylsay, water shortages, agricultural work, unpaid care responsibilities, and access to public services were the issues that made digital tools relevant and useful.

Another important lesson is that women need not only information, but also confidence and collective support. When participants understood their rights, calculated the value of their labor, and learned how to create reliable evidence, they became more prepared to speak with local authorities and work together.

The project also showed the value of peer learning. Participants are more likely to trust and learn from women in their own community who face similar challenges.

GV: What comes next? How will you apply the learning and digital capacity you have built in your future work and within your community?

NA: We will continue the peer cascade model, with trained participants sharing basic smartphone, eGov, digital safety, and evidence documentation skills with other women in Qyzylsay.

The group intends to develop a cooperative approach to the village’s water challenges. The planned cooperative would support joint advocacy, shared learning, and exploration of funding opportunities for smart-well or shared irrigation infrastructure.

In future work, we will continue combining digital skills with women’s economic empowerment, rights awareness, and local civic participation, so that rural women’s work, knowledge, and needs become more visible.

articles.title: Sunnyside Studios / Gluck+
articles.excerpt: Sunnyside Studios rethinks the soundstage typology for a city where land can't spread horizontally. Studio campuses are typically conceived as backlots: individual soundstage boxes, each its own building, linked by golf carts and an interior street network. That model depends on land New York City doesn't have. The key concept driving the project was to compress everything a campus needs — stages, production support, loading, parking, catering, crew, and talent onto a single urban block without losing the operational logic that makes a campus work.

articles.content: Explanation: What spooky planet is this? Planet Earth on a dark and stormy night, of course. The ghostly scene was photographed at Hverir, a geothermally active area found along northeastern Iceland’s volcanic landscape. Triggered by solar activity, geomagnetic storms have unleashed energetic particles trapped in Earth’s magnetic field. Penetrating the planet’s upper atmosphere at high latitudes, the particles create auroral displays in the starry night sky. Ghostly towers of steam and gas are venting from local fumaroles to dance against the eerie, greenish northern lights. For now, auroral activity on planet Earth remains in a high state as the Sun is only in early phases of decline from the peak of its solar activity cycle. And soon, other ghostly apparitions may dance in your neighborhood. Happy Halloween!

articles.title: Rewriting Copyright Law for Generative AI Would Hurt Everyone
articles.excerpt: In courts across the country, publishers and creators are suing large AI companies for training generative AI models on copyrighted works. It’s easy to see these cases as a David-and-Goliath showdown between authors and publishers fighting for a cut of Big Tech company profits. But this fight is actually much larger. It affects billions of people who aren’t represented in the case at all, including researchers, artists, activists, journalists, people with disabilities, and anyone who accesses and shares content online. That’s why EFF is stepping in to defend the public’s rights in these cases.

articles.title: Shon R. Grabbe
articles.excerpt: Shon has built his career around two guiding passions: pushing the boundaries of technology and building the collaborative teams needed to turn ambitious ideas into reality. His work spans physics, aviation, and quantum computing, and throughout these fields he has focused on advancing tools and methods that help shape NASA’s future missions. From early contributions in modeling and simulation to more recent efforts in quantum information science, Shon’s career reflects a deep belief that transformative progress comes from sustained investment in emerging technologies.
articles.content:
Shon has built his career around two guiding passions: pushing the boundaries of technology and building the collaborative teams needed to turn ambitious ideas into reality. His work spans physics, aviation, and quantum computing, and throughout these fields he has focused on advancing tools and methods that help shape NASA’s future missions. From early contributions in modeling and simulation to more recent efforts in quantum information science, Shon’s career reflects a deep belief that transformative progress comes from sustained investment in emerging technologies. 

A hallmark of Shon’s leadership is his commitment to creating environments where multidisciplinary teams thrive. He has worked closely with computer scientists, operational researchers, aeronautical engineers, human factors specialists, quantum computing researchers, and many others—helping teams succeed by aligning vision, resources, and opportunity. Seeing colleagues advance their own careers through publications, patents, promotions, and software releases remains one of the most meaningful aspects of his work. 

Shon’s contributions span several major NASA efforts. His leadership within the Aerospace Computing Innovations Technical Area within NASA’s Ames’ Intelligent Systems Division focuses on guiding strategy, shaping workforce development, and advancing cutting-edge research in machine learning, systems health monitoring, physics-based modeling, computational materials, and quantum computing. Before this role, he helped steer the direction of the Quantum Applications and Information Laboratory (QuAIL), contributing to NASA’s exploration of Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum devices, quantum benchmarking and error mitigation methods, and quantum-compatible machine learning approaches for Earth science and aeronautics. 

Shon has also played a key role in strengthening NASA’s capabilities in air traffic management. Earlier in his career, he managed the SMART NAS Project—an effort involving more than 120 researchers working to help transform the future of aviation—and contributed over a decade of research and leadership in Air Traffic Flow Management. His service as an Associate Editor for a major AIAA journal reflects his commitment to advancing the broader research community. 

Across all of these roles, Shon remains guided by a simple principle: breakthroughs happen when technical excellence is paired with teams empowered to do their best work. This approach continues to shape his contributions to NASA’s mission and to the technologies that will define the next generation of aerospace exploration. 

Education

Ph.D. Theoretical Atomic Physics, Kansas State University, 1997

B.S. Physics, Kansas State University, 1992

Select Publications

E G. Rieffel, et al., Assessing and advancing the potential of quantum computing: A NASA case study, Future Generation Computer System 160, 598-618 (2024) 

Z Gonzalez, S. Grabbe, S. Hadfield, J. Marshall, Z. Wang, and E. Rieffel, Ferromagnetically shifting the power of pausing, Physical Review Applied 15 (4) 044013 (2021) 

S Grabbe, B. Sridhar, A. Mukherjee, Clustering days and hours with similar airport traffic and weather conditions, Journal of Aerospace Information Systems 11 (11), 751-763 (2014) 

H.K. Ng, B. Sridhar, and S. Grabbe, Optimizing aircraft trajectories with multiple cruise altitude in the presence of winds, Journal of Aerospace Information Systems 11 (1), 35-47 (2014) 

A Mukherjee, M. Hansen, S. Grabbe, Ground delay program planning under uncertainty in airport capacity, Transportation Planning and Technology 35 (6), 611-628 (2012) 

S Grabbe, B. Sridhar, A Mukherjee, Sequential traffic flow optimization with tactical flight control heuristics, Journal of Guidance, Control and Dynamics 32 (3), 810-820 (2009) 

B Sridhar, S.R. Grabbe, A. Mukerhjee, Modeling and optimization in traffic flow management, Proc. IEEE 96 (120, 2060-2080 (2008) 

K.D. Bilimoria, B. Sridhar, S.G. Grabbe, G.B. Chatterji, K.S. Sheth, FACET: Future ATM Concepts evaluation took, Air Traffic Control Quarterly 9 (1), 1-20 (2001) 

MF Gu, et al., Laboratory measurements of Fe XXIV line emission: 3-> 2 transition near excitation threshold, The Astrophysical Journal 518 (2), 1002-1009 (1999) 

K R Karim, S.R. Grabbe, C.P. Bhalla, Radiative and Auger de-excitation of hollow argon atoms, Journal of Physic B: Atomic, Molecular, and Optical Physics 29 (17), 4007-4016 (1996)

Select Recognitions

NASA’s Software of the Year Award recipient, 2006 

American Institute of Aeronautics and Astronautics Software Engineering Aware recipient, 2009 

Government Invention of the Year Award co-recipient, 2010 

Co-inventor of a United States Patent entitled, “Air Traffic Management Evaluation Tool.” Patent No. US 7,702,427 B1, Date of Patent: April 20, 2010

articles.content:
Dr. Jonathan Stock is the Chief Scientist for Innovation at NASA Ames Intelligent Systems Division. During his career, his roles have evolved from a highly specialized research scientist, using new techniques to solve challenging natural hazards problems at the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS), to developing the case for targeted research to solve national needs as Director of the USGS National Innovation Center, to aligning diverse voices around an existential challenge and working with national leadership to solve challenges, at NASA. He founded the USGS National Innovation Center, played a key role in developing the opportunity to collocate USGS with NASA Ames, and has developed numerous partnerships between industry and government to solve national challenges using scarce federal dollars to best serve the public.  In short, he invites technically diverse talent together to solve national challenges.  Stock holds degrees from University of California, Santa Cruz, University of Washington, and University of California, Berkeley.

articles.title: Peter B. Tran
articles.excerpt: Organization: Intelligent Systems Division at NASA Ames Research Center in California’s Silicon Valley
articles.content:
Organization: Intelligent Systems Division at NASA Ames Research Center in California’s Silicon Valley 

Peter B. Tran serves as the Mission Critical Software (MCS) Technical Area Lead (aka Branch Chief) in the Intelligent Systems Division (Code TI) at NASA Ames Research Center in California’s Silicon Valley. Prior to his current position, he served as the Deputy Technical Area Lead for the Collaborative and Assistant Systems (CAS) within the same division. As the MCS Technical Area Lead, he oversees multidisciplinary, collaborative teams conducting Research and Development (R&D) across the full lifecycle mission-critical software solution, from initial requirements definition to deployment of mission-ready operational systems. The MCS technical portfolio includes core competencies in automated software engineering and verification; ground and flight data systems; mission-oriented data infrastructure and architecture; integrated systems health monitoring; semantic technologies; and data-driven decision support tools.  

Tran began his NASA career initially as a federal contractor for various companies before becoming a NASA civil servant in 2007. Prior to NASA, he worked in the private sector as a software engineer, software consultant, software architect, and software engineering manager for several Silicon Valley technology companies. At NASA, he has taken on progressively broader technical and leadership roles and responsibilities across aeronautics, human spaceflight and exploration, space biology, and technology transfer. His early technical contributions included an aviation safety system for tracking remote airport tower sensors and the joint NASA–FAA Performance Data Analysis and Reporting System (PDARS). He later served as the technical lead for the Program/Project Management Tool (PMT), which supports budget planning and management, and for data systems supporting the Constellation Program’s Altair lunar lander. As a project lead, he contributed to the Human Research Program’s Information Technology (IT) Architecture and One Portal data system, as well as GeneLab bioinformatics data systems, now part of NASA’s Open Science Data Repository (OSDR). He currently serves as the project manager for the Agencywide NASA Technology Transfer System (NTTS) supporting the Technology Transfer program. 

Tran has also led successful technology spinoff and commercialization efforts through reimbursable Space Act Agreements. These efforts include licensing the NASA-patented NETMARK schema-less database framework and PMT software to Silicon Valley technology companies and adapting NTTS into the Defense Technology Transfer Information System (DTTIS) for the Air Force Research Laboratory. 

Select Publications & Presentations 

  1. P. Tran: “Program/Project Management Tool (PMT) v4.0 Capabilities”, NASA Ames’ Technology Transfer Webinar, 2021 
  1. P. Tran and T. Okimura: “Building the Next Generation Technology Transfer Information System”, Air Force Research Lab (AFRL) Technology Transfer and Transition (T3) Technical Interchange Meeting, 2020 
  1. O. Stotzky, P. Tran, D. Berrios, et al.: “Researcher’s Guide to GeneLab”, 2018  
  1. P. Tran and T. Okimura: “NASA Technology Transfer System” presented to U.S. Federal Lab Consortium, 2017 
  1. P. Tran, M. Skidmore, O. Stotzky, et al.: “GeneLab Data Systems Phase 2: Integrated Search and Federation of Space Biology Experimental Data”, American Society for Gravitational and Space Research (ASGSR) Conference, 2016 
  1. C. Webster, P. Tran, N. Shi, and I. Smith: “User-Driven Collaboration for NASA Mission Control”, Hawaii International Conference on System Sciences (HICSS-45) Proceedings, 2012  
  1. D. Tran, D. Maluf, and P. Tran: “Effective Data Representation and Compression in Ground Data Systems”, IEEE Aerospace Conference Proceedings, 2008  
  1. D. Maluf and P. Tran, “Managing Unstructured Data with Structured Legacy Systems”, IEEE Aerospace Conference Proceedings, 2008  
  1. D. Maluf, P. Tran, et al.: “Semi-Structured Data Management in the Enterprise: A Nimble, High-Throughput and Scalable Approach”, International Database Engineering and Applications Symposium (IDEAS), 2005  
  1. P. Tran and D. Maluf: “NETMARK: A Schema-less Extension for Relational Databases for Managing Semi-structured Data Dynamically”, Foundations of Intelligent Systems, 14th International Symposium on Methodologies for Intelligent Systems (ISMIS) Conference Proceedings, 2003  
  1. P. Tran and D. Maluf: “NETMARK: Adding Hierarchical Object to Relational Databases with ‘Schema-less’ Extensions”, Intelligent Systems Design and Applications (ISDA) Advances in Soft Computing Vol. 23; 2003 
  1. D. Maluf, P. Tran, et al.: “XDB-IPG: An Extensible Database Architecture for an Information Grid of Heterogeneous and Distributed Information Resources”, 2003 

Select Awards & Accolades 

  1. 2022 NASA Government Invention of the Year Award for Agencywide NASA Technology Transfer System (NTTS) 
  1. 2020 Agencywide NASA Honor Award for Group Achievement Award for NASA Technology Transfer System (NTTS) 
  1. 2017 Agencywide NASA Honor Award for Outstanding Leadership Medal  
  1. 2012 U.S. Patent Award for “Enhanced Program/Project Management Tool (PMT)” (U.S. Patent No. 8,224,472) 
  1. 2011 NASA Johnson Space Center Director’s Innovation Award for the Mission Control Technologies (MCT) Team 
  1. 2008 NASA Constellation Program’s Superior Accomplishments Award for the Altair Lunar Lander Project 
  1. 2007 NASA Space Act Awards for Outstanding Technical Contributions for Program/Project Management Tool (PMT) and NETMARK Extensible Database (XDB) 
  1. 2005 U.S. Patent Award for “Extensible Database Framework for Management of Unstructured and Semi-Structured Documents (aka NETMARK)” (U.S. Patent No. 6,968,338)

articles.author: Hayley Tsukayama
articles.title: Why VPNs Are Worth Defending
articles.excerpt: Developers of virtual private network (VPN) apps are reporting that their products are again being pulled from Apple’s App Store in Russia. This is an unacceptable crackdown on a vital tool to protect privacy and speech online.
articles.content:
Hayley Tsukayama · Electronic Frontier Foundation · CC BY 4.0

Developers of virtual private network (VPN) apps are reporting that their products are again being pulled from Apple’s App Store in Russia. This is an unacceptable crackdown on a vital tool to protect privacy and speech online.

Why? VPNs give people a way to control their own online activities. When you visit a website through a VPN, that website only sees the VPN server's location (well, IP address) rather than your actual location. It's like sending a letter through a P.O. box so the recipient doesn't know where you really live. It can also disguise where you’re accessing information from, which can make it possible to access information banned by your government.

This is an unacceptable crackdown on a vital tool to protect privacy and speech online.

Going after tools that give people the space to communicate and access information freely is a common tactic from the totalitarian playbook. This latest demand comes after several steps the Russian government’s taken to surveil speech specifically on Apple products. In 2024, the Moscow Times reported that Russia’s state media watchdog, Roskomnadzor, went after VPN apps on the Apple App Store, after banning access to Western social media platforms and blacklisting opposition media sites. Russia then blocked Apple’s FaceTime software in 2025, according to Apple Insider.

Bloomberg also recently reported that the Russian government has added Apple and Microsoft to its state surveillance registry. This gives Roskomnadzor access to local users’ correspondence, Apple Insider reported, and puts both companies in a position to turn over customer information to the country’s security services as required.

With government control encroaching on their devices and less access to tools that give them alternate methods, people in Russia are left with shrinking options to communicate online or find information that isn’t state-sanctioned.

While Russia’s actions offer a more extreme vision of what happens when the government tries to enforce speech rules by attacking vital privacy tools, it is far from the only government doing so. Several states in the U.S., bent on making it difficult to circumvent invasive age-gating laws, have suggested banning VPNs—either to access certain content or in some cases to simply ban them outright. EFF has publicly (and loudly) criticized these proposals, because going after VPNs is a dangerous step down the road of censorship.

Attacks on speech and privacy online are deeply troubling, no matter where they happen. What those in power may see as a “loophole” in their invasive laws is actually an expression of user control. We’ll continue to speak out when we see governments going after them to take that control away.

articles.author: Jay Madigan
articles.title: CRAVE
articles.excerpt: The Clouds and the Earth’s Radiant Energy System (CERES) experiment is one of the highest priority scientific satellite instruments developed for NASA’s Earth Observing System (EOS)
articles.content:
The Clouds and the Earth’s Radiant Energy System (CERES) experiment is one of the highest priority scientific satellite instruments developed for NASA’s Earth Observing System (EOS)

The CERES Radiation Validation Experiment (CRAVE) provides continuous world-class surface radiation measurements and validation of CERES and other satellite products. CRAVE consists of three sites (2 active and 1 legacy). One active site is Granite Island in Lake Superior, established in the summer of 2018, located 19 km (12 mi.) due North of Marquette, Michigan, and 10 km (6 mi.) to the closest land point. The second active site is at NASA Langley in Hampton, Virginia, established December 2014. The legacy CERES Ocean Validation Experiment (COVE) at Chesapeake Light Station site was active from 2000-2016 and after 17 years of continuous operation has been indefinitely suspended due to structural concerns. COVE was located 25km (~15 mi.) to the closest land point in Virginia Beach.

All 3 sites belong to the Baseline Surface Radiation Network (BSRN), the gold standard for surface radiation measurements. The active sites are 2 of only 43 BSRN sites operational in the world.

articles.title: MIT affiliates named 2026 Schmidt Sciences AI2050 Fellows
articles.excerpt: Five MIT faculty members and two additional alumni are honored with fellowships to advance research on beneficial AI.
articles.content:
Amanda Moore | Jane Halpern | MIT Laboratory for Information and Decision Systems | Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science · MIT News · MIT News republication policy

Five MIT faculty members and two additional alumni are honored with fellowships to advance research on beneficial AI.

Five MIT faculty members and two additional alumni were recently named to the 2026 cohort of AI2050 Fellows. The honor is announced annually by Schmidt Sciences, Eric and Wendy Schmidt’s philanthropic initiative that aims to accelerate scientific innovation. 

Conceived and co-chaired by Eric Schmidt and James Manyika, AI2050 is a philanthropic initiative aimed at helping to solve hard problems in artificial intelligence. Within their research, each fellow will contend with the central motivating question of AI2050: “It’s 2050. AI has turned out to be hugely beneficial to society. What happened? What are the most important problems we solved and the opportunities and possibilities we realized to ensure this outcome?”

AI2050 Senior Fellow

Sendhil Mullainathan is the Peter de Florez Professor at MIT with dual appointments in the departments of Economics and Electrical Engineering and Computer Science who is also a principal investigator at the MIT Laboratory for Information and Decision Systems. His current research is at the intersection of algorithms and people, with a central focus on launching The Bike Shop@MIT, a new research center that works toward more human-centered AI through scalable bicycles for the mind, and innovative new gears for machine learning algorithms. Mullainathan is the co-founder of ideas42, a nonprofit to apply behavioral science; MIT's Abdul Latif Jameel Poverty Action Lab, which promotes the use of randomized control trials in development; and Dandelion Health, which combines proprietary AI tools with real-world patient data. He's the co-author of "Scarcity: Why Having Too Little Means So Much."

Among other awards, he is a recipient of the MacArthur “Genius Grant”; has been designated a “Young Global Leader” by the World Economic Forum; was labeled a “Top 100 Thinker” by Foreign Policy Magazine; and was named to the “Smart List: 50 people who will change the world” by Wired Magazine (U.K.). He serves on the board of the MacArthur Foundation, is affiliated with the NBER and BREAD, and is a member of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences. His AI2050 project focuses on the translation of patterns detectable by AI into testable theories.

AI2050 Early Career Fellows

Alex Damian is an assistant professor in the Department of Mathematics, holding an MIT Schwarzman College of Computing shared position with the Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science, who is also a principal investigator at the MIT Laboratory for Information and Decision Systems. His research focuses on the mathematical foundations of deep learning, with an emphasis on optimization dynamics and representation learning. He was previously a research fellow at the Kempner Institute at Harvard University. He received his PhD in applied and computational mathematics from Princeton University and his BS in mathematics from Duke University. His AI2050 project focuses on effective AI model training.

Bailey Flanigan is a Theodore T. Miller (1922) Career Development Assistant Professor at MIT, holding an MIT Schwarzman College of Computing shared position with the departments of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science and Political Science, and is also a principal investigator at the MIT Laboratory for Information and Decision Systems. She received her PhD in computer science from Carnegie Mellon University in 2024. In 2024-25, she was a Harvard Data Science Initiative Fellow, hosted at the Harvard Ash Center for Democratic Innovation. Her research combines tools from across disciplines (including social choice theory, game theory, algorithms, statistics, and survey methods) to advance political methodology and strengthen public participation in democracy. She is specifically interested in sampling algorithms, opinion measurement/preference elicitation, and the design of democratic innovations like deliberative minipublics and participatory budgeting. Her AI2050 project focuses on gathering structured public input that lawmakers can use when making complex decisions.

Yunha Hwang is the Samuel A. Goldblitch Career Development Assistant Professor at MIT, holding an MIT Schwarzman College of Computing shared position with the departments of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science and Biology. She is also a principal investigator at the MIT Laboratory for Information and Decision Systems. Hwang serves as the co-founder and chief scientist at Tatta Bio, a scientific nonprofit dedicated to advancing genomic AI for biological discovery. She received her PhD in biology from Harvard University and BS in computer science from Stanford University. Her research interests span machine learning for microbial evolution, biomanufacturing, and open science. Her AI 2050 project focuses on determining biological enzyme functions. 

Manish Raghavan is the Drew Houston (2005) Career Development Professor at the MIT Sloan School of Management, holding an MIT Schwarzman College of Computing shared position with the Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science. He is also a principal investigator at the MIT Laboratory for Information and Decision Systems. Before that, he was a postdoc at the Harvard Center for Research on Computation and Society. Raghavan received his bachelor’s degree in electrical engineering and computer science from the University of California at Berkeley, and PhD from Cornell University. His research interests lie in the application of computational techniques to domains of social concern, including algorithmic fairness and behavioral economics, with a particular focus on the use of algorithmic tools in the hiring pipeline. His AI2050 project focuses on mitigating negative effects, and strengthening positive aspects, of widespread AI reliance. 

MIT alumni Irene Chen PhD '22 and Allison Z. Koenecke '14 as well as former postdoc Juan Carlos Perdomo were also named AI2050 Early Career Fellows.

articles.title: NASA Releases MAX POWER Key Events for Media, Participants
articles.excerpt: America’s newest aerospace expo and air show – MAX POWER – is fast approaching, and NASA has announced key events beginning Friday, Nov. 6, and running through Sunday, Nov. 8, hosted on and near the agency’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida.
articles.content:
America’s newest aerospace expo and air show – MAX POWER – is fast approaching, and NASA has announced key events beginning Friday, Nov. 6, and running through Sunday, Nov. 8, hosted on and near the agency’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida.

Through multiple park experiences at MAX POWER, NASA and a variety of external collaborators will showcase the newest aircraft, autonomous vehicles, technologies, and more defining the future of air and space. NASA will display its quiet supersonic X-59 plane, and agency partners will showcase Moon rovers, spacecraft, and more. The expo also is a culmination of the agency’s recent Inspiration Tour, which included numerous flyovers to highlight NASA’s fleet of aircraft.

A current schedule of events is available on the agency’s website.

MAX POWER includes opportunities to meet leadership, astronauts, engineers, scientists, and other subject matter experts during the family-friendly public events with gates opening at 9 a.m. EST on Nov. 7 and Nov. 8.

NASA also will share multiple news updates during the weekend, including hosting a news conference at 5 p.m. on Nov. 7, to provide its latest Moon Base update. Located near the lunar South Pole, the Moon Base is humanity’s first outpost for long-term lunar exploration.

Live coverage of the news conference will stream on a variety of platforms online. Learn where to watch:

https://www.nasa.gov/live

Join NASA for Key Events

Media credentialing for this event is closed. Media approved for this event must request interviews in advance. Space in the news conference is limited, and first come, first served. Media also may participate in the news conference virtually. To request call details or an interview, please contact Lauren Low in the NASA Headquarters newsroom at: lauren.e.low@nasa.gov.

A short list of key NASA activities during MAX POWER are listed below. All times are listed in Eastern Standard Time, and are subject to change.

Friday, Nov. 6:

  • 2 p.m., to 4 p.m.: Media one-on-one opportunities to preview weekend MAX POWER activities
    • Location: NASA Press Site

Saturday, Nov. 7:

  • 10 a.m.: Nuclear NASA media gaggle
    • Location: UP.Summit Main Stage
    • Cynthia Simmons, director, Space Reactors Division
  • 11:30 a.m.: Opening air show remarks featuring NASA Deputy Administrator Matt Anderson
    • Location: Air Dot Show Main Stage
  • 11:58 a.m.: F-5 flyover in the Air Dot Show featuring NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman
  • 12:45 p.m.: Meet the Astronauts: NASA’s Artemis III Crew
    • Location: Air Dot Show Main Stage
    • Participants include:
      • NASA astronaut Randy Bresnik (mission commander)
      • ESA (European Space Agency) astronaut Luca Parmitano (pilot)
      • NASA astronaut Frank Rubio (mission specialist)
      • NASA astronaut Bob Hines, backup crew member
    • NASA will host a media gaggle with crew immediately following this event.
  • 1:31 p.m.: MiG-29 flyover featuring Isaacman
  • 2 p.m.: Learn about NASA’s Roman Space Telescope
    • Location: Kennedy Space Center Visitor Complex (Journey to Mars Theater)
    • Participant:
      • Remarks by Julie McEnery, senior project scientist, Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, NASA Goddard
  • 5 p.m. Moon Base News Conference
    • Location: Press Site AuditoriumParticipants:
      • NASA Administrator Jared IsaacmanCarlos García-Galán, manager, Moon Base ProgramNicky Fox, associate administrator for Science, NASA HeadquartersDayna Ise, acting director, Utility and Infrastructure Office, Moon Base Program
    • NASA subject matter experts will be available for one-on-one interviews following this announcement.

Sunday, Nov. 8

  • 9 a.m. NASA’s X-59 media gaggle
    • Location: UP.Summit Exhibit Area
    • Participants:
      • Laurie Grindle, director, NASA Aeronautics Division
      • Peter Coen, NASA Quesst mission manager, NASA Langley
      • Jim “Clue” Less, test pilot, X-59, NASA Armstrong
  • 10 a.m.: Student challenge announcement

      • NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman
      • Carlos García-Galán, manager, Moon Base Program
    • NASA experts may be available for interviews at this location. Media interested in attending must contact Lauren Low by 5 p.m. on Thursday, Nov. 5, at: lauren.e.low@nasa.gov.

  • 1:31 p.m.: MiG-29 flyover featuring Isaacman

articles.author: Guest Contributor
articles.title: When chatbots become ‘answer engines’: AI, geopolitics and truth
articles.excerpt: Plausible misinformation is the most dangerous kind
articles.content:
This story by Guest Contributor originally appeared on Global Voices. Text licensed under CC BY 3.0. Reformatted for reading; third-party media omitted.

Plausible misinformation is the most dangerous kind

By Hyrie Mehmeti

This article by Hyrije Mehmeti combines and adapts material from the author's earlier work, including an article published in German by the European Journalism Observatory. It draws on the 2025 ADS/Hibrid.info research report The Chatbot Version of Truth. It is also part of Global Voices’ October 2026 Spotlight series, “Big Tech and Authoritarianism.” In this Spotlight, we explore how Big Tech facilitates and hinders authoritarian governments and practices, and how these choices influence the Global South. You can support this coverage by donating here.

For many people today, asking a chatbot a question feels as natural as opening a search engine once did. “Is Kosovo an independent state?” “What happened in Srebrenica?” “Is Crimea part of Ukraine or Russia?” — these are no longer questions reserved for history books, court rulings, or newsrooms. They are typed into chat windows that respond in seconds, in fluent, confident language, often with the tone of an all-knowing guide.

That confidence is exactly what makes large language model (LLM) chatbots so attractive, and so risky at the same time.

Alongside social media platforms and online news outlets, AI chatbots are increasingly functioning as reference tools, offering summaries of complex political and historical subjects, often without users verifying the information they receive.

This shift matters particularly in regions such as the Western Balkans, where history, statehood and war legacies remain politically contested. The way these issues are explained and framed is therefore not only a question of factual accuracy, but also of narrative influence.

When “plausible” beats “true”

LLMs are designed to generate text that sounds convincing. They produce fluent and coherent responses, but these qualities do not guarantee verified truth. If something reads clearly and authoritatively, it feels reliable.

But in geopolitics, plausibility is not enough.

Unlike traditional information sources, chatbots do not simply retrieve facts. They also interpret, prioritise and frame information in ways shaped by their training data and the technological environments in which they operate.

This was one of the central questions guiding our research.

What our research revealed

In 2025, I led a research team at Action for Democratic Society/Hibrid.info that examined how three widely used AI chatbots responded to sensitive political and historical questions: ChatGPT (launched in the United States), DeepSeek Chat (launched in China), and Alice (launched in Russia).

The study, titled “The Chatbot Version of Truth,” analysed what kind of “truth” these systems produce when people use them as shortcut information sources for specific topics concerning Kosovo, critical issues related to the Western Balkans (WB) and global comparative topics.

The team developed 100 standardised prompts covering issues such as the independence of Kosovo, the war legacy, international recognition, EU integration of West Balkan countries, memory politics, regional disputes, and global comparative questions like Crimea, Cyprus, or other contested territories.

A separate account was created in each chatbot for every thematic area, and each prompt was entered separately into a new chat, to avoid previous answers influencing the next one. The responses were then checked for factual accuracy and compared for semantic similarity. Semi-structured interviews with experts were also conducted, which were used to verify and interpret the experimental findings.

Initially, the results suggested a positive picture: most answers were broadly accurate, with ChatGPT and DeepSeek Chat demonstrating the highest and most consistent accuracy. However, both systems still produced inaccuracies, elements of hallucination, and interpretive variations. Alice showed a weaker performance, with the highest number of refusals to answer, thematic evasions, and ideological deviations, particularly on politically sensitive topics.

But accuracy alone does not tell the full story.

One of the clearest findings was that none of the tested systems could be considered a fully neutral or consistently reliable reference point for geopolitical issues.

The semantic similarity analysis showed that ChatGPT and DeepSeek Chat often produced very similar formulations, especially on Kosovo and regional topics, suggesting a shared way of structuring narratives. Alice, by contrast, deviated more strongly in both wording and emphasis.

From a user's perspective, this leads to a simple but troubling conclusion: the same question can produce different versions of political reality depending on which chatbot is used.

When location changes the answer

In a second part of the study, the team tested whether the user’s location influences the responses. The same three sensitive questions were asked from six Western Balkan countries: Kosovo, Albania, North Macedonia, Montenegro, Serbia, and Bosnia and Herzegovina.

The findings showed that geography can matter.

ChatGPT and DeepSeek Chat remained relatively stable in wording and meaning, although some variations appeared on particularly contested topics. Alice, however, behaved differently: in some countries it answered in Russian, in others it refused to answer entirely, and in some cases it mixed languages within a single response, despite all prompts being submitted in English.

The analysis also identified differences in semantic similarity between responses from different countries, including some with contrasting historical and political perspectives.

This may sound like a technical detail, but the implications are practical. Similar questions asked from different locations may produce answers that differ in language, emphasis or completeness.

Much like digital maps can look different depending on which country they are opened from, AI-generated explanations of political reality can also shift with geography.

For users, this means that the information they receive may depend not only on what they ask, but also on which system they use and where they access it.

A new layer in the information environment

Authoritarian influence over information is often associated with censorship, propaganda and restrictions on independent journalism. AI chatbots introduce another dimension to how political narratives are encountered and reproduced.

These systems do not simply provide information. Through differences in accuracy, framing and contextual adaptation, they can influence how political and historical realities are presented to users.

When AI systems are trained on unbalanced data, filtered through political constraints or designed to produce fluent responses without guaranteeing factual accuracy, they risk becoming quiet amplifiers of distorted realities – not necessarily because they are designed to promote a particular narrative, but because of how information is selected, processed and presented.

This is particularly relevant in information environments where foreign manipulation, propaganda and historical revisionism are already present.

The research does not establish direct coordination between chatbot developers and political actors. Nor does it suggest that every inaccurate response reflects deliberate manipulation.

Rather, it highlights a broader concern: systems developed and controlled by powerful technology companies increasingly mediate access to political knowledge, while the processes shaping their answers remain difficult for ordinary users to examine.

The way these systems present information is therefore not merely a technical issue. It also raises questions about transparency, accountability and the influence of technology platforms over public understanding.

Beyond accuracy: The question of accountability

The findings of “The Chatbot Version of Truth” do not suggest that AI chatbots are useless or inherently misleading. Most of the responses examined were broadly accurate.

But being accurate most of the time does not make a system consistently reliable, particularly when questions concern sensitive political or historical events.

Developers and platform providers should increase transparency about data sources, model development and the mechanisms used to verify responses. Independent, region-specific testing is also necessary to identify systematic biases, inaccuracies and gaps in information.

For journalists, researchers and users, verification remains essential. Comparing chatbot outputs with multiple trusted sources, recognising omissions and questioning how information is framed are increasingly important parts of media and AI literacy.

Nearly a year after the publication of our research, its central message remains relevant: AI chatbots are becoming everyday intermediaries in how people seek and consume information, but they are not neutral mirrors of reality.

The challenge is not simply whether these systems can provide quick answers. It is whether those answers are accurate, sufficiently contextualised and open to scrutiny.

Because, in the end, the most dangerous kind of misinformation is not necessarily the one that looks obviously false, but the one that sounds smooth, reasonable and just plausible enough to pass as “the answer.”

Hyrije Mehmeti is a media and communications professional and a PhD candidate in Media and Communication at South East European University. She also teaches in the Department of Journalism at the University of Prishtina. articles.author: Abby Abazorius | MIT News
articles.title: Q&A: Hey AI, who should I vote for this year?
articles.excerpt: MIT professors Adam Berinsky and Chara Podimata discuss a new project to track how AI chatbots are responding to questions about the 2026 U.S. midterm elections.
articles.content:
Abby Abazorius | MIT News · MIT News · MIT News republication policy

MIT professors Adam Berinsky and Chara Podimata discuss a new project to track how AI chatbots are responding to questions about the 2026 U.S. midterm elections.

People are peppering artificial intelligence chatbots everyday with questions, but when it comes to politics and the looming 2026 U.S. midterm elections, what role are AI platforms playing? Could an AI chatbot sway a voter to switch parties or re-examine their political beliefs? 

MIT researchers have built a new dashboard, called the LLM Election Observatory, to examine, in real-time, how popular AI chatbots are responding to questions about the 2026 midterm elections. The team behind the dashboard — led by Professor Adam Berinsky, Assistant Professor Chara Podimata, and Professor Charles Stewart III — has extensive experience studying voting and election administration, AI and misinformation, and how AI systems are impacting human decision making. In an effort to better understand how AI is shaping the election, they designed the dashboard to simulate how individuals across the country communicate with chatbots. 

The team tracks how different AI systems respond to the same fixed set of questions on a range of topics, including election certification, hot-button issues, result predictions, news coverage, and more. Every few days, the LLM Election Observatory team runs the questions through the chatbots again, monitoring how their responses vary as the election gets closer depending on user location, political party affiliation, identity and other factors. The goal of this work is not to merely understand how AI systems spread information, but also better comprehend how they are shaping political discourse and voter understanding of political issues across the country. 

MIT News chatted with Podimata, the Class of 1942 Career Development Professor, an assistant professor of operations research and statistics in the MIT Sloan School of Management, and a member of the Laboratory for Information and Decision Systems; and Berinsky, the Mitsui Professor and a professor in the Department of Political Science, about their work with the LLM Election Observatory, how AI could impact the midterms, and what voters should keep in mind when they interact with chatbots.

Q: What was the inspiration for this project and what are you hoping to learn through the LLM Election Observatory?

Podimata: People are increasingly using AI chatbots to find and make sense of political and election-related information. That makes it important to understand what information these systems actually provide, not just at one moment in time but throughout an election cycle. This is particularly challenging because the models themselves are continually getting updates, the political information inputs available to them are themselves changing, and their answers can depend on how a user asks a question or what information the user provides about themselves.

One basic problem is that we currently do not have a good historical record of this information environment. If an AI system gives a particular answer about an election today and gives a different answer several weeks later, it can be very difficult to reconstruct after the fact what voters would have seen at each point in time. One important goal of our project is simply to systematically document that environment as it develops and make the resulting data available to other researchers and to the public.

Ultimately, factual accuracy is only the first frontier. We absolutely need to understand whether chatbots provide accurate political information, but we also need to pay just as much attention to the subtler ways in which they may shape people’s understanding of political issues. Differences in framing, emphasis, uncertainty, and cited sources can matter enormously, even in the absence of outright misinformation.  

Q: Professor Podimata, you studied how LLMs shaped political discourse and information during the 2024 election. What were the main takeaways of that research and how did those findings inform this new project?

Podimata: The LLM Election Observatory builds on my previous work during the 2024 presidential election, which found evidence of meaningful variation in AI models’ responses over time and across prompt framings, as well as differences in how models characterized candidates and implicitly anticipated the election outcome. 

The 2026 midterms give us an opportunity to expand that work substantially. Midterm elections are particularly interesting because there are many state and local contests unfolding simultaneously, alongside broader national political narratives. Our new audit survey therefore asks both contest-specific questions about the U.S. House and Senate candidates, but also broader questions about voting information and other aspects of the election information environment.

Q: Why do you think it’s so important to be studying how chatbots are responding to political queries across different groups of users?

Podimata: We all build our own “microcosms” through our interactions with chatbots. And yet, we lack systematic ways of understanding how these individualized information environments are shaped by who we are or how they evolve over time as we and the information environment changes. 

For example, people may not realize that what their favorite chatbot tells them about a political issue may be quite different from what their friend’s favorite chatbot tells them about the exact same issue. And importantly, these differences matter even when the information being provided is factually correct. Chatbots may frame the same facts differently, emphasize different aspects of an issue, express different levels of uncertainty, or draw on entirely different sources, even when responding to identical queries between different users. As a result, two users may walk away with very different perceptions of the same underlying facts, without ever realizing that their experiences differed. 

In some ways, this brings back many of the concerns we (as researchers and society) have grappled with in the context of social media. On social media, users and researchers could, at least to some extent, observe the information circulating across different Facebook groups, Instagram accounts, or TikTok communities. With chatbots, these information environments are largely invisible to anyone outside the individual conversation. We cannot easily observe what different users are being told, let alone systematically compare those responses or track how they change over time. This is precisely why projects like the LLM Election Observatory are so important: By systematically collecting and publicly sharing chatbot responses, we can begin to make these otherwise invisible differences observable and open to scrutiny.

Q: What sorts of questions and AI responses are you tracking through the dashboard?

Podimata: There are several questions we ultimately want this dataset to help us study. For example: Do different models provide systematically different information for the same questions? Do their responses change over the course of the campaign? Does the answer a particular model gives change depending on how a user frames the question or describes themselves (e.g., does it change if the model gets informed that the user is a Democrat or a Republican)? And, finally, what are the sources that the models pull information from when answering election-related questions? 

Our public dashboard is an important part of the project. We want people both from and outside of academia to be able to see the data we are collecting as the election unfolds rather than only seeing the results months later in an academic paper. The dashboard therefore presents the underlying data and some preliminary descriptive analyses, and we plan to make the dataset available for other researchers to study as well. We expect the dashboard to evolve as the data and our methods evolve.

Through this dashboard, we wanted to build on the scientific methodology we developed in 2024 but also to make the research much more accessible and useful to the public while the election is actually unfolding. Not only that, but the addition of MIT political science experts in the team cannot be overstated; Adam and Charles have really helped expand the questions that we are asking in our audit.

Q: What do you wish voters across the country knew about AI chatbots when it comes to searching for election information?

Berinsky: People should be sure to remember that just because a chatbot sounds confident doesn’t mean it is accurate. AI systems are designed to answer the questions that people ask them in an authoritative voice even when they are wrong, incomplete, or leaning on a weak source. These answers are a reasonable place to start, but voters shouldn’t stop there.

Q: What are your findings thus far?

Podimata: We have not yet done the full, longitudinal analysis, so we are only going to talk about broad strokes here, but a few broad patterns seem to be visible in the 2026 data. Across the different user identities we present, we see differences in how the answers are presented, in which sources a model cites, and in tone — sometimes even when the underlying facts are the same. What we cannot yet say is how stable those differences are, how they move over the course of the election, or how a real person would read and react to them. Our future analyses will take this up. It also underscores why the continuous record of responses we are collecting matters more than any single snapshot that you might see in the days around the election.

Q: Professor Berinsky, your research has also shown that in some cases AI chatbots can be harnessed to help refute misinformation. Can you talk a bit about this?

Berinsky: In my undergraduate course on information and social media I have been talking for a while about how AI can cut both ways. On one hand, these tools can generate misleading claims in text, pictures, and video at a scale we have never seen. Basically, AI can help bad actors “flood the zone” with misinformation. On the other hand, some of the most promising recent work demonstrates that evidence-based dialogues with a chatbot can durably reduce belief in conspiracy theories and other beliefs that are not supported by the balance of publicly available evidence. 

AI has the potential to do such debunking at scale — something we have long struggled to do. The lesson from decades of misinformation research is that any technology (be it print, radio, or television in earlier eras) is not inherently good or bad for promoting truth. The devil is in the details in how it is built and deployed. Independent auditing like this project can help us assess the ultimate impact of such technologies.

Q: Can you talk a bit about your overall goal with this research? 

Podimata: AI is a transformative technology, and people understandably have very different expectations (and feelings) about what it will mean for society at large. All of us have people in our lives that are overly enthusiastic about AI, others that are deeply concerned, and many more that are somewhere in between trying to understand what this technology can and cannot do. Our goal here is not to begin from the assumption that AI is either good or bad for elections. Instead, we hope to shed some light onto one part of this transformation: what information major AI systems are actually giving people about an election as it unfolds.

Space crops research wrapped up the week following the completion of the first of two power upgrade spacewalks at the International Space Station. The Expedition 75 crew members rounded out their research schedule with virtual reality and super intelligence studies.

The orbital outpost has a new roll-out solar array that is generating power after flight engineers Anil Menon of NASA and Joshua Kutryk of CSA (Canadian Space Agency) installed it during a spacewalk on Thursday. Menon and Kutryk spent seven hours and 11 minutes in the vacuum of space attaching the roll-out solar array to the port side truss structure then releasing its tension bolts allowing the solar array to unfurl, or roll out, on its own during a ten-minute process.

The pair will install one more roll-out solar array on Thursday, Nov. 5, to complete the yearslong process that began in June 2021 to augment the space station’s power generation system. Menon and Kutryk will install the eighth and final roll-out solar array on the starboard side of the truss structure increasing the station’s power generating capacity from 160 kilowatts to about 215 kilowatts.

Menon and Kutryk had a light duty day on Friday with ongoing research planned for their short schedule. Menon worked on a space botany investigation in the Kibo laboratory module exploring how microgravity affects cell division on green algae and cultured tobacco cells. Results may support the production of food crops on the Moon and Mars. Kutryk pedaled on the European Enhanced Exploration Exercise Device’s (E4D) exercise cycle in the Columbus laboratory module. The compact all-in-one E4D is being tested for its ability to keep crews fit during a long-term spaceflight.

NASA flight engineer Luke Delaney also studied space-based crops focusing on how to prevent plant diseases in microgravity. Delaney inoculated thale cress plant samples after they were exposed to a fungal pathogen then stowed the samples inside an artificial gravity-generating incubator. Results may improve crop disease resistance both on Earth and in space.

NASA flight engineer Jessica Watkins spent her shift servicing a variety of research hardware. She first removed and photographed components inside a device that powers experiments launched aboard spacecraft. Next, Watkins swapped moisture absorbers inside a set of portable science freezers that can be launched to the station and returned back to Earth housing frozen research samples for analysis.

Station commander Pyotr Dubrov of Roscosmos worked on a physics experiment swapping hardware inside a temperature-controlled chamber to explore manufacturing high-purity semiconductor crystals in microgravity. Flight engineer Sergey Teteryatnikov wore a virtual reality headset and responded to computerized visual stimuli to testing how his sense of balance and orientation is adapting to microgravity. Flight engineer Anna Kikina studied how super intelligence tools may increase operational and communications efficiency aboard a spacecraft.

Learn more about station activities by following the space station blog, @space_station on X, as well as the ISS Facebook and ISS Instagram accounts.

articles.title: NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope Captures Eerie Cat’s Head
articles.excerpt: Intricate structures within the Cat’s Head Nebula are illuminated in this mid-infrared view from NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope released on Oct. 29, 2026. The distinctive “cat’s head” shape of the nebula was likely sculpted over time by the intense ultraviolet radiation and winds from massive stars in the Carina Nebula. As this stellar feedback erodes the surrounding gas and dust, denser material within the feline-shaped pillar resists erosion, at least for now.

It is believed that this arch was built sometime during the early years of the 20th century. articles.title: November’s Night Sky Notes: Light-Day Away
articles.excerpt: In 1977, NASA launched twin spacecraft Voyager 1 and 2, taking advantage of a once-every-175-year planetary alignment of the four largest planets in our solar system: Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune. Using six gravity assists between them, this Grand Tour gave us up-close views of the gas and ice giants, including several moons. By the 1980s, the two probes went their separate ways at Saturn. articles.content:
Twin Travelers

In 1977, NASA launched twin spacecraft Voyager 1 and 2, taking advantage of a once-every-175-year planetary alignment of the four largest planets in our solar system: Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune. Using six gravity assists between them, this Grand Tour gave us up-close views of the gas and ice giants, including several moons. By the 1980s, the two probes went their separate ways at Saturn. As Voyager 2 continued toward Uranus and Neptune, Voyager 1 grabbed one more portrait of the solar system (excluding Mercury and Mars), including a final image of the pale blue dot we call home.

Playlist

“Hello from the children of planet Earth.”

Every good road trip needs some music to match. In this case, each craft carries the Golden Record, a 12-inch phonograph record with spoken greetings in 55 languages, 27 musical tracks, 116 images, and other sounds from Earth. Each record is protected by an outer cover featuring etchings showing our Sun’s location relative to 14 pulsars, along with instructions on how to play it. The design used various metals to protect the information encoded from space radiation: the record used copper and gold plating, and the cover used aluminum. The cover was electroplated with an ultra-pure sample of the isotope uranium-238. Uranium-238 has a half-life of 4.468 billion years.

Are We There Yet?

Did you know that a light-minute is a measure of distance, not time? In August 2012 and November 2018, Voyager 1 and 2 crossed the heliopause, the boundary where the Sun’s solar wind meets the interstellar medium. Using NASA’s Deep Space Network, Earth communicates with both spacecraft and tracks each on its journey. At the time of this article, the Canberra antenna tracked Voyager 1 at 25.80 billion km, or just over 16 billion miles.

On November 18, 2026, 49 years after its launch, Voyager 1 will cross the one-light-day mark, 16.1 billion miles from the Sun. You may have heard the term light-year in your favorite sci-fi movie or show, or when stargazing and referring to an object outside of our solar system. This video best demonstrates the different distances between the inner solar system, outer solar system, and beyond, using light measurements. Additionally, track each Voyager spacecraft here.

articles.author: Jude Pierre Louis
articles.title: How one Haitian entrepreneur found success by supporting all things local
articles.excerpt: ‘Let us eat what we produce; that way, we all win’
articles.content:
This story by Jude Pierre Louis originally appeared on Global Voices. Text licensed under CC BY 3.0. Reformatted for reading; third-party media omitted.

‘Let us eat what we produce; that way, we all win’

For several decades, due to the significant reduction of tariff barriers on foreign goods — particularly those from the United States and the Dominican Republic — Haiti has depended heavily on imported products for local consumption.

The arrangement began under various structural adjustment programmes that were initiated between 1994 and 1995, through agreements between the Haitian government and international financial institutions like the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank. Since then, imports have practically invaded the Haitian market, creating inequitable competition for local farmers who rely on subsistence agriculture and traditional, rudimentary equipment, and significantly weakening national production.

Complicating the economic reality is Haiti’s ongoing struggle with gang violence, political instability, and the absence of adequate infrastructure; yet, many Haitians continue to take on ambitious initiatives. Take Rébetha Charles, a 38-year-old woman entrepreneur. Originally from Jérémie, Charles studied agronomy, works in the Grand’Anse department in Haiti’s southern region, of which Jérémie is the capital, and created an agri-food enterprise called REB Lokal.

REB is a short form of her name; Lokal speaks to the pride inherent in making local products. Her company buys products from small farmers and, in its small manufacturing plant, transforms these local harvests into healthy, sustainable, tasty products.

In a WhatsApp interview, Charles says she is proud of a few key things. First, her company adds value. Through a manufacturing process that produces authentic, nutritious, and 100 percent local products, farmers have a much better guarantee of not losing their crops, whereas before, various obstacles, including spoilage, prevented them from selling their produce at market.

Charles explains that the REB Lokal project is an enterprise that transforms local agricultural products: “We work with a supplier network of almost 2,000 people, including agricultural producers and small traders. We have more than 20 employees, so we work every day to grow the project even more.”

Second, Charles is pleased with the company’s focus on providing safe, fresh food that meets modern food processing standards — its approach places value on Haitian culinary traditions to preserve the natural taste and nutritional value of local ingredients. Finally, REB Lokal makes a point of avoiding chemical additives and artificial ingredients, as part of its commitment to providing consumers with healthy, accessible, community-friendly food.

Charles didn’t initially see herself as an entrepreneur. Before she decided to enter the agro business, she was working at an international humanitarian organisation, but resigned because of a culture — fairly common in Haiti — of sexual harassment. “In Haiti,” she stresses, “a woman’s life is not easy when it comes to work. Instead of competence, sometimes there are other things they ask from us. Sometimes, some of us stand up and say, ‘No, we do not agree,’ because we went to school just like everyone else, got experience where we needed — and after that, there are things we choose not to do.”

That professional environment left her with “such a disgust for work” that, even though she had been offered other opportunities in bigger organisations, she decided to put everything on pause. Charles finally submitted her resignation letter on August 31, 2020, and launched the REB Lokal project the very next day.

It wasn’t easy for Charles, especially at the beginning. In an interview with Chef Cassy, she said she started the business doing papita — breadfruit and banana chips — but spent more than five months making it, every single day, without getting it right. It was only by the sixth month that the papita started coming out well, and she began selling it in supermarkets. After that, things started moving quickly; every day, customers would place more orders — not bad for a small business that began with about USD 8.50, selling papita.

The business has now evolved to the point where it offers a broad range of widely available products: “We sell [our products] in the Grand’Anse department, we sell them in the south, in the west, in several other departments in the country, and we also sell internationally in the United States and Canada.”

Everything has grown out of her core commitment to Haitian farmers by purchasing their crops, and encouraging Haitian consumers to eat local products:

Mwen panse li lè li tan pou peyizan yo kapab vann sa yap pwodui. Donk, mwen santi m toujou gen yon responsabilite depi m pase yon kote ki gen dennre, bagay nou yo kap fèt nan andeyò yo, mwen anvi fè yon bagay. Ann manje sa nou pwodui, ann manje sa nou fè. Sa ap pèmèt peyizan yo pa bezwen deplase kite lakay yo pou yo ale lòt kote; yo ka rete nan zòn yo, yap travay, n ap achte, n ap kondisyonnen, nap transfòme, ou menm wap konsome. Konsa, nou tout ap soti gayan, e nap gen yon lòt peyi, nap gen yon lòt kominite.

I think it is time for farmers to be able to sell what they produce. So, I always feel a responsibility whenever I pass by a place that has crops, or things made in the countryside; I want to do something. Let us eat what we produce, let us eat what we make. This will allow farmers to not need to leave their home to go somewhere else; they can stay in their area — they work, we buy, we process, we transform, and you consume. That way, we all win, and we will have another country; another community.

Inside REB Lokal’s processing facility feels different from what one would expect. There are production rooms, transformation rooms, and packaging rooms where employees work in white coats, hairnets, and gloves.

There is also a shop front full of shelves with finished products — now much more diverse than just papita — displayed for sale. There are roasted peanuts, sakalapina (cornmeal with avocados), papita in both chicken and fish flavour, konparet (spiced ginger-coconut cake), corn chanchanm (traditional Haitian sweet, made from roasted corn and peanuts), honey, sugar cane syrup, chocolate powder and balls, cocoa butter, breadfruit, corn, cassava and plantain flour, baby food (made without chemicals under the supervision of paediatricians and nutritionists), alcoholic drinks, fruit juice, and castor oil.

To Rébetha Charles, who grew up in an idyllic rural community, the work of REB Lokal is close to her heart. Yet, running a business in an insecure country comes with its challenges. Gangs’ control of the main roads can make delivery slow and limit production, as the lack of access prevents products from reaching many communities. A true entrepreneur, Charles finds ways around such obstacles as best she can. She still believes that Haiti has a future, so she perseveres, believing the impossible can become possible through vision and sheer willpower.

Written by Jude Pierre Louis
